title: Who Will Win as AI Rewrites Competitive Advantage?
gist: BCG argues AI's real story is not productivity but a redistribution of value pools: a $750B/yr hyperscaler capex cycle several times more GDP-intensive than the 2000 telecom build-out has installed a permanent 'compute layer' that taxes every adopting sector, while equity markets have already erased ~$2T from legacy enterprise software ahead of any reported earnings damage. The central risk it names is 'hollowing' — revenue, share and retention stay intact while AI-native attackers strip out the highest-margin layer of the value chain.

insights.claim: Hyperscaler capital expenditures are on track to reach $750 billion in 2026 alone, and the cumulative 2026-2031 AI build-out will rank as one of the most concentrated capital reallocations in modern economic history.
insights.speaker: BCG Henderson Institute
insights.so_what: Sizes the demand pool for chips, power and grid equipment; deceleration in this single line item is the dominant swing factor for AI-levered equities.
insights.quote: Hyperscalers' capital expenditures are on track for $750 billion in 2026 alone.
insights.locator: The Capital Reallocation Has No Modern Parallel

insights.claim: Measured as capital expenditure as a percentage of GDP, the AI build-out runs several times the intensity of the telecom industry's build-out at the turn of the millennium.
insights.speaker: BCG Henderson Institute
insights.so_what: The telecom analogy cuts both ways: it frames the macro growth impulse and simultaneously invokes the canonical overbuild precedent to stress-test against.
insights.quote: in terms of capital expenditure as a percentage of GDP, it is several times the intensity of the telecom industry’s build-out at the turn of the millennium
insights.locator: Measured cumulatively from 2026 through 2031

insights.claim: The AI boom's spoils so far have gone narrowly to suppliers of the physical foundation — chip designers, memory and equipment makers, gas-turbine and grid suppliers with order books stretching beyond 2029, and utilities and landlords holding scarce grid-connected power.
insights.speaker: BCG Henderson Institute
insights.so_what: Order books visible past 2029 make power generation and grid supply the most contracted, least speculative leg of the AI trade.
insights.quote: gas-turbine and grid suppliers with order books stretching beyond 2029
insights.locator: So far, the spoils of the AI boom

insights.claim: The derating of legacy enterprise software has already wiped roughly $2 trillion in market value from companies whose subscription moats once looked impregnable.
insights.speaker: BCG Henderson Institute
insights.so_what: A concrete gauge of how much AI-disruption risk is already in the price — the benchmark for judging whether SaaS derating is finished or just starting.
insights.quote: The derating of legacy enterprise software has wiped some $2 trillion in market value off companies whose subscription moats once looked impregnable.
insights.locator: But equity markets have already begun voting

insights.claim: IT services, media and outsourcing valuations have compressed on margin fears that have not yet appeared in reported earnings, meaning markets are pricing the disruption in advance rather than waiting for it.
insights.speaker: BCG Henderson Institute
insights.so_what: Fundamentals lag the tape here; screening on trailing earnings in these sectors will look cheap right up until the margin erosion prints.
insights.quote: Markets are not waiting for AI to disrupt these sectors; they are pricing the disruption in advance.
insights.locator: At the same time, values of IT services

insights.claim: The compute layer is a structurally new claimant that takes a share of every AI-enabled transaction and becomes a permanent new line in most companies' P&L, analogous to how electric utilities became a permanent intermediary in every industrial process in the early 20th century.
insights.speaker: BCG Henderson Institute
insights.so_what: Model AI adoption as a recurring claim on adopters' output rather than one-off capex — it structurally caps how much of the AI dividend can reach end-user sectors.
insights.quote: AI's compute layer plays the same role: a claimant on the output of every sector that adopts it, and for most companies, a permanent new line in the P&L.
insights.locator: The arrival of compute as a structural beneficiary

insights.claim: Five structural factors determine AI value capture within a sector: task substitutability, market concentration and data defensibility govern who gets the value, while compute intensity and regulatory friction govern how fast it transfers and how much leaks out of the sector entirely.
insights.speaker: BCG Henderson Institute
insights.so_what: A five-variable screen for sector-level AI winners that discriminates far better than a blanket 'AI adopter' label.
insights.quote: Three govern direction, determining who gets the value: task substitutability, market concentration, and data defensibility. Two govern speed and leakage
insights.locator: As for the value within a sector

insights.claim: The same AI technology produces opposite outcomes depending on sector structure: financial services oligopoly plus regulation lets shareholders retain most of the surplus, retail hypercompetition passes nearly all of the AI dividend to consumers within a handful of years, health care value flows to consumers, and pharma splits it between consumers and shareholders as discovery costs fall.
insights.speaker: BCG Henderson Institute
insights.so_what: Fade AI margin capture in competitive retail; shareholder capture is strongest where concentration and regulation persist — but the article flags that financial-services regulatory moat as narrowing.
insights.quote: In retail, hypercompetition forces almost all of the AI dividend through to consumers within a handful of years.
insights.locator: This framework produces strikingly different outcomes

insights.claim: Because the same foundation models and inference economics are broadly available, the underlying technology converges to parity within two to three years, pushing durable advantage downward to the assets and structures beneath the technology.
insights.speaker: BCG Henderson Institute
insights.so_what: Puts a two-to-three-year clock on model-based differentiation — pay for underlying assets and data flows, not for model access.
insights.quote: the underlying technology converges to parity within two to three years
insights.locator: Which Advantages Will Survive?

insights.claim: The most precarious competitive advantages are the ones that were previously deep enough to feel permanent but are now fragile under AI: knowledge and expertise, stock data, and operational excellence.
insights.speaker: BCG Henderson Institute
insights.so_what: A short-list of moat types to fade — expertise-billing and static-dataset businesses look intact on reported metrics while eroding externally.
insights.quote: These are the advantages most likely to look intact from the inside while eroding from the outside.
insights.locator: The most precarious quadrant is the bottom right

insights.claim: Flow data compounds in a way stock data cannot, illustrated by Visa's VisaNet processing more than 257 billion transactions a year that continuously improve its fraud and authorization models.
insights.speaker: BCG Henderson Institute
insights.so_what: Forces a distinction between continuously-generated proprietary data flows and static archives when underwriting any 'we have the data' moat claim.
insights.quote: Visa's VisaNet processes more than 257 billion transactions a year, informing fraud and authorization models that improve with each one.
insights.locator: Flow data—continuously generated by a product

insights.claim: System-level integration and scarce physical assets are the moats AI strengthens rather than erodes, exemplified by BlackRock's Aladdin platform, Amazon's million-robot fulfilment network, and Caterpillar's autonomous-mining fleet running on its own software.
insights.speaker: BCG Henderson Institute
insights.so_what: Names a concrete long list of AI-amplified rather than AI-threatened incumbents: embedded workflow platforms and asset-heavy operators that own their software stack.
insights.quote: BlackRock's Aladdin platform was a moat before AI, and embedding AI deepens it.
insights.locator: System-level integration turns single-process tools

insights.claim: Midscale incumbents get compressed from both sides — large enough to carry legacy cost but too small to own a data flywheel or network scale — so two companies in the same sector under the same macro scenario can land on opposite sides of a profit-pool shift.
insights.speaker: BCG Henderson Institute
insights.so_what: Argues for barbell positioning within sectors — true-scale leaders plus AI-natives — and against the mid-tier where sector index exposure concentrates the damage.
insights.quote: Midscale incumbents—large enough to carry legacy cost but too small to own a data flywheel or network scale—are compressed from both sides.
insights.locator: This enables incumbents with true scale

insights.claim: The most dangerous AI dynamic is 'hollowing': revenue, market share and customer retention all look intact while margin and pricing power drain away, so the damage stays invisible in headline numbers until it reaches the P&L.
insights.speaker: BCG Henderson Institute
insights.so_what: Track gross margin and price per unit of work, not revenue or share — top-line stability is a lagging and actively misleading indicator of AI disruption.
insights.quote: The moat looks intact from the inside; from the outside, it has been crossed.
insights.locator: The most dangerous dynamic of all

insights.claim: The AI-native attacker's structural edge is organizational rather than technological — no embedded headcount, committed real estate or inherited workflow — which drives a far lower cost base in knowledge-intensive functions and reduces the minimum viable scale at which a segment becomes profitable.
insights.speaker: BCG Henderson Institute
insights.so_what: Explains why incumbent AI adoption closes only part of the gap, and why previously unservable niches abruptly become attackable profit pools.
insights.quote: bolting AI onto a legacy operation closes only part of it, because architecture and talent, rather than tools, drive the advantage
insights.locator: Which AI-Native Competitor Is Targeting Your Margin?

insights.claim: The most dangerous attackers do not undercut incumbents on price to take share; they isolate the highest-margin component of the value chain, sell it standalone, and leave the incumbent the low-margin remainder — which makes market share the wrong metric for assessing the threat.
insights.speaker: BCG Henderson Institute
insights.so_what: Share-based competitive screens systematically miss the threat; look instead at where margin concentrates inside a value chain and whether that layer is separable.
insights.quote: the attacker competes for margin, not revenue—invisibly because the competitor set is defined by share
insights.locator: The standard incumbent playbook assumes

insights.claim: Pre-AI precedents show the margin-extraction mechanism clearly: Chime owns the customer relationship and interchange economics while chartered banks hold the deposits and payment infrastructure, and retail media networks such as Amazon's extract advertising margins of 70% to 90% while the retailer fulfills product at low single-digit margins.
insights.speaker: BCG Henderson Institute
insights.so_what: The 70-90% versus low-single-digit split quantifies how lopsided layer capture can be — a template for sizing any AI attacker's opportunity against an incumbent's P&L.
insights.quote: allow the platform that controls what the customer sees to extract advertising margins of 70% to 90%, while the retailer fulfills the actual product at low single-digit margins
insights.locator: The digital-era precedents make the pattern clear

insights.claim: AI attackers are already running the layer-capture play: Augury optimizes uptime on equipment it does not build in order to capture the after-market service margin OEMs have historically owned, while customer-service agents Sierra and Decagon price per successful resolution rather than per seat, leaving incumbents the hard escalated cases.
insights.speaker: BCG Henderson Institute
insights.so_what: Outcome-based pricing is the tell — it detaches vendor revenue from seat counts and attacks the incumbent's highest-margin service line directly.
insights.quote: AI agents like Sierra and Decagon resolve interactions autonomously and set prices based on the outcome: per successful resolution rather than per seat
insights.locator: AI now runs the same play

insights.claim: AI strategies should be pressure-tested against three specific rewrite risks: compute proving more expensive than the business case assumes, equity-market repricing sharper than the capital plan allows, and access to frontier models becoming conditional on geopolitical factors.
insights.speaker: BCG Henderson Institute
insights.so_what: Names the three tail risks that would break the consensus AI-adoption case; compute-cost inflation and export-control shocks are the two with observable market triggers.
insights.quote: A bet that pays off in only one scenario is a gamble, not a strategy.
insights.locator: Make bets with your eyes open

insights.claim: A company's equity multiple relative to its sector is a readable verdict on whether the buy-side has classified it as a winner or loser in AI's value redistribution, and in the absence of a clear signal from management the market writes that narrative itself.
insights.speaker: BCG Henderson Institute
insights.so_what: Relative multiple dispersion within a sector becomes a fast screen for which names the market has already condemned — and where that verdict may be wrong.
insights.quote: If your multiple has compressed relative to your sector, the market sees you as a loser in the redistribution; if it has expanded, it sees you as a winner.
insights.locator: Articulate the narrative for shareholders

insights.claim: The bottleneck to executing an AI strategy is rarely the technology but talent, workflows and culture, so the incumbents that struggle will be those whose organizations cannot metabolize AI rather than those lacking access to it.
insights.speaker: BCG Henderson Institute
insights.so_what: Diligence should weight organizational redesign and talent flow above AI spend or tooling announcements when separating genuine adopters from theater.
insights.quote: The incumbents that struggle will not be the ones that lack the technology; they will be the ones whose organization cannot metabolize it.
insights.locator: Redesign the organization for AI-first execution
